name: Emeka Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don’t sell anything or campaign. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal day at work like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Emeka Larsen, 27, and I lead a line crew for an electricity company. We meet at the old relay shed by the canal, check permits and tools, then drive to the job; I climb when the crew needs another pair of experienced hands.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What makes a good day, and what part takes the most out of you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A good day is when we find the fault, make the repair, and get homes back on without rushing a safety step. Cold rain and a long drive wear me down, and I have less than a month of expenses saved despite being a team lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a program can tidy the outage notes, but it cannot see a cracked insulator from the road. We still have to inspect the pole ourselves before we decide what to isolate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little office help probably won’t change how many call-outs the crew gets. My bigger worry is still the thin pay against rent and fuel, especially when my old van needs work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d use the note tool only after checking the outage details against what we saw at the relay shed. I’d keep my normal rota and take lunch from home twice a week to build a small repair fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The software change feels small enough to handle with a proper check. The money pressure is still there, and I don’t like having no room if the van fails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you postpone if you had to pay for a van repair this month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d delay buying a new phone and stop getting breakfast on the road. My partner Elise and I rent a small flat, so I’d talk with her before using any of our shared bill money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the small AI change make you feel safe about the household budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it only leaves the job mostly as it is. I feel fairly safe about the crew’s work in this picture, but not comfortable about our savings.

say: I’d say a tool can tidy **outage notes**, but it cannot spot a cracked insulator from the road.
I want our crew to keep checking each **pole in person**.
think: A small office tool probably leaves our **call-out work** unchanged.
Rent, fuel and my aging van still strain the **household budget**.
do: Check every **outage note** against what the crew saw on site.
Keep my rota and **bring lunch from home** twice each week.
feel: I feel **steady about work**, but uneasy about having no repair cushion.
S0.quote: We still have to inspect the pole ourselves before we decide what to isolate.
fieldNote: Emeka trusts **hands-on inspection** over tidied records and ties safety to an actual site visit.
His calm outlook on work coexists with **thin savings** and vehicle costs.

steps.text: Check outage notes against the crew’s observations before isolation
Bring lunch from home twice a week
Set aside the lunch money for van repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI can arrange the work orders faster, but the crew lead still has to check the actual access and weather at a site. I’d want the company to explain whether faster dispatch means fewer paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some planning and records are part of my job, so I could lose those duties even while the climbing remains. If office work gets cheaper, I’m not sure the company will keep the same number of crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d try the new dispatch system after an experienced supervisor had checked it, and I’d ask to learn its safety alerts. I’d keep my field skills current and record my hours each month so I could notice a cut early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious because fewer shifts would hit us quickly, and there aren’t many other utility crews nearby. I’ll learn a system once it has been proven, but I don’t want to trust an untested safety prompt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your crew if an automated work order looked incomplete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell them not to leave the shed until the missing permit and isolation details were checked. I’d ask the supervisor to log the fault so the system doesn’t keep sending bad orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would applying to another utility protect your income if they all use similar systems?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might give me another crew for a while, but it would not protect the planning duties from the same change. I’d look at posted field openings only after I knew the pay and travel distance.

say: I’d say AI may arrange **work orders**, but I still check site access and weather.
I would ask whether faster dispatch means **fewer paid shifts** for my crew.
think: Planning and records are among the **duties I could lose**.
I worry the company might use cheaper planning to send out **fewer crews**.
do: Try dispatch alerts after an experienced **supervisor checks them**.
Keep field skills current and **record my monthly hours**.
Ask the supervisor to **log incomplete work orders**.
feel: I feel **anxious** because fewer shifts would quickly strain our budget.
S1.quote: Some planning and records are part of my job, so I could lose those duties even while the climbing remains.
fieldNote: He recognizes **planning exposure** inside his lead role despite the hands-on nature of the job.
He accepts tested tools but requires **safety checks** and clear hours from management.

steps.text: Learn the dispatch system’s safety alerts after supervisor review
Keep current field skills and inspect job sites
Record monthly hours and set aside any extra pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say our planning, records and fault diagnosis cannot be treated as protected jobs once that system arrives. There is a gap before robots, but I would not tell anyone the crew has a secure future just because the pole work lasts longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the company may cut lead duties quickly, then reduce field crews when robots arrive in 2031. I don’t know whether I’d be chosen for a different post, and my savings would not carry me very far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the company now to pay for a practical electrical safety instructor course while I still draw wages. In 2029 I’d apply for real instructor openings, but I’d check whether the role is mostly lesson writing or hands-on teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious because I can take steps now, though I can’t know how many jobs will remain. I would worry much more if a manager named my crew for cuts; until then, I’m not assuming the worst is certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Elise about the two years before AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell Elise we should keep the flat and avoid borrowing for a nicer van while my job is uncertain. I’d ask her to look at our budget with me, and we could decide whether to build a little more cash first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Instructor work includes planning and teaching. Is that a protected career after full AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, lesson writing and diagnosis are thinking work too, so I can’t promise myself that the instructor role survives. It might be a bridge if an actual vacancy exists, and I would still need to consider what hands-on jobs remain before 2031.

say: I would say our planning, records and diagnosis are **not protected work** after full thinking AGI.
I see the time before robots as a **short transition**, not a guarantee for our crew.
think: I think lead duties may shrink first, followed by **field crews** in 2031.
A new post is uncertain, and my **savings are limited**.
do: Request company funding for a **practical safety instructor course** now.
Apply for genuine instructor openings in **2029** and check the duties.
Review the **household budget with Elise** before taking on debt.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but able to take steps before any confirmed cuts.
S2.quote: I don’t know whether I’d be chosen for a different post, and my savings would not carry me very far.
fieldNote: He expects meaningful risk to **lead and crew work**, but does not claim a certain personal dismissal.
He questions instructor work as a **temporary possibility**, not a safe destination.

steps.text: Request company funding for an electrical safety instructor course
Apply for real instructor openings in 2029 and check lesson duties
Keep the current flat and avoid borrowing for a newer van

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives a crew time to learn new procedures and see what the company actually plans. It doesn’t make planning and diagnosis safe after 2031 or pole work safe after robots arrive in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with two years, I can finish a qualification and put away more than pocket change. I would still worry about whether an instructor post is there when the computer can write its lessons and answer the trainees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for the course details in writing this winter and set an automatic small transfer after payday. In 2032 I’d apply for openings that include practical demonstrations, after asking who hired graduates and what they paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, although the extra time lets me check each step instead of jumping at the first offer. It does not add employers to this area or make moving cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see before you enrolled in that course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want a real qualification, a timetable that fits around call-outs, and a supervisor who can explain the practical assessment. I’m not paying for a vague promise about being future-proof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for work if a suitable opening appeared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d consider moving if the job and salary were written down and Elise wanted to come too. We’d need enough money for the deposit and travel, and I don’t have that saved yet.

say: I would say five years gives our crew time to learn **new procedures** and hear company plans.
I would not call planning protected after 2031 or line work after **2034**.
think: I can complete training and save **more than pocket change**.
I think instructor vacancies may shrink when AI writes **lessons and answers trainees**.
do: Get written **course details** and arrange a small automatic transfer.
Apply in **2032** for practical instructor openings after checking graduate outcomes.
Consider moving only with a **written job offer** and Elise’s agreement.
feel: I feel **anxious but deliberate**, because time helps me check options.
S3.quote: I’m anxious, although the extra time lets me check each step instead of jumping at the first offer.
fieldNote: He sees extra time as room to **verify a course**, not a promise of work.
Limited savings and **few local employers** constrain any move with Elise and raise its upfront cost.

steps.text: Get written details for the electrical instructor qualification
Transfer a small amount to savings after payday
Apply for practical instructor openings in 2032 after checking outcomes
Move only if Elise agrees and a written job offer covers costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years is a fair warning to train and save steadily, but the company still needs to tell us what it expects to automate. The thinking parts change in 2036, and the robot date comes later in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d have time to finish a certificate, build a reserve, and speak with Elise before considering a move. Still, I can’t count on instructor work after 2036 because AI can do planning and teaching as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d take a recognized safety instructor course in small units and aim to save toward three months of bills. In 2037 I’d look for posts with practical equipment demonstrations and confirm the wages before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels more workable than two, but I’m not comfortable yet because the savings are so low. A long warning helps me decide gradually; it doesn’t cover next month’s rent or a van repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Elise notice you changing this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She’d notice that I set aside money on payday and use one evening for the first course unit. We’d keep the flat while I check whether the qualification leads to a real opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you see instructor work as permanently safe once AGI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the job has lesson planning and diagnosis, so it is exposed too. I’d treat an instructor role as one option to investigate, not a promise that my income is settled.

say: I would use ten years to **train and save**, and ask the company to share its plans.
I would tell our crew thinking work changes in 2036 and robots follow in **2039**.
think: I can finish a course and build a **cash reserve** gradually.
Instructor work includes exposed planning, so I cannot rely on it **permanently**.
do: Take a recognized **safety instructor course** in small units.
Save toward **three months of bills** and check the balance regularly.
Review practical instructor posts in **2037** and confirm wages.
feel: I feel **more able to prepare**, though current low savings still worry me.
S4.quote: A long warning helps me decide gradually; it doesn’t cover next month’s rent or a van repair.
fieldNote: The longer horizon supports **gradual action**, but does not erase current rent and vehicle costs.
He treats instruction as an option and recognizes its **thinking-task exposure**.

steps.text: Complete a recognized line-safety instructor course unit by unit
Save toward three months of household bills
Review practical instructor vacancies and confirm wages in 2037
Keep the current flat with Elise while checking whether a vacancy exists

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because there is little time before planning tasks change and only until 2031 before robots arrive. Paid training during work hours, honest staffing information, and enough pay to build savings would give me a better chance to choose carefully.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether lineworkers will be involved in testing equipment that changes our safety steps. People who know the poles and weather should be heard before a new system is trusted in the field.

headlineQuote: People who know the poles and weather should be heard before a new system is trusted in the field.
portrait: Emeka is a **27-year-old senior lineworker** who leads a crew and values careful repairs.
He has **under one month saved** and few similar local jobs.
He adopts technology once proven and wants **supervised practical instruction** for safety tools.
He uses warning time to **train and save**, while seeing office and physical work as exposed on different dates.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** gives little time before planning changes and robots arrive in 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training**, honest staffing information and enough income to build savings would help.
